challenge_query: (tendinopathy OR "achilles" OR "low back pain" OR sciatica OR "disc herniation" OR "neck pain" OR radiculopathy OR "groin pain" OR "anterior cruciate ligament" OR "hamstring" OR "musculoskeletal pain" OR "sports injury") AND (placebo OR sham OR injection OR corticosteroid OR "platelet-rich plasma" OR surgery OR surgical OR medication OR "wait and see" OR "natural history" OR "no treatment" OR overtreatment OR "low-value care" OR "diagnostic accuracy" OR reliability) AND (PUB_TYPE:"randomized controlled trial" OR PUB_TYPE:"systematic review" OR PUB_TYPE:"meta analysis" OR PUB_TYPE:"practice guideline")
challenge_focus: Pick the papers most likely to contradict, limit or replace what a sports and musculoskeletal physiotherapist usually does with active adults and athletes. Wanted: null or negative trials of exercise, manual therapy, education, load management or other common physiotherapy; trials where injection, medication, surgery, placebo, sham or no treatment did as well as or better than rehabilitation; evidence that a common clinical test, strength test or outcome measure is unreliable or inaccurate; natural-history, overtreatment and low-value-care evidence. Leave out papers that mainly confirm exercise or physiotherapy works, surgical technique comparisons with no conservative arm, anaesthesia and perioperative analgesia, cost-effectiveness analyses, protocols, and paediatric, neurological, cancer or pregnancy populations.
focus: Private-practice sports and musculoskeletal physiotherapy with active adults and athletes. Rank first, in this order: (1) Achilles tendinopathy, discogenic low back pain, referred or radicular neck pain, adductor-related groin pain; (2) other tendinopathy (patellar, hamstring, gluteal), ACL and knee rehabilitation, hamstring and running injuries; (3) other low back or neck pain trials relevant to a physiotherapist. Wanted content: exercise and load management, rehabilitation dosing, return to sport, education, prognosis, outcome measures and strength testing, and trials of injections, medication, surgery, needling or passive modalities for these conditions, because they bear on when rehabilitation is or is not the right choice. Rank a well-run trial with a null or negative result as highly as a positive one. Leave out: surgical technique comparisons, anaesthesia, nerve blocks and perioperative analgesia; health-economic and cost-effectiveness analyses; paediatric, elderly-frailty, neurological, cancer and pregnancy populations; qualitative-only or methods-only reviews. Prefer randomised trials, systematic reviews and guidelines that could change or confirm treatment.
